title: Purcell-Engineered Hybrid Coupler for Leakage-Suppressed Robust CZ Gates
authors: Hui Wang, Feng Bao, Yan-Jun Zhao, Xun-Wei Xu
abstract: We propose a Purcell-engineered notch-filter hybrid coupler for superconducting controlled-$Z$ (CZ) gates that combines coherent interaction engineering with leakage-selective dissipation. The architecture integrates a nonlinear transmon coupler with a coupled Purcell-filter and notch-resonator subsystem, providing additional control over both the coherent interaction pathways and the engineered dissipative environment. The filter branch reshapes the effective interaction pathways, while the notch resonator further tailors the frequency response of the coupled filter network and preserves strong leakage-selective dissipation.   Using dressed-eigenstate analysis together with Lindblad master-equation simulations, we show that the proposed architecture substantially reduces leakage and improves the worst-case computational-state fidelity compared with an optimized single-transmon coupler while remaining robust over a broad range of coherence assumptions and device parameters. The optimized gate achieves $F_{\rm avg}=99.74\%$, $F_{\rm min}=99.62\%$, and a maximum leakage probability of $1.6\times10^{-3}$. These results demonstrate that engineered dissipation complements conventional coherent interaction engineering and provides an additional design degree of freedom for realizing robust, high-fidelity superconducting CZ gates.
summary: The paper introduces a novel Purcell-engineered hybrid coupler designed to enhance the robustness of CZ gates in superconducting quantum processors. By integrating both coherent interaction engineering (via the transmon coupler) and leakage-selective dissipation (using filter/notch resonators), the authors achieve state-of-the-art gate fidelities while drastically suppressing unwanted energy loss pathways.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing robust superconducting controlled-Z (CZ) gates by effectively suppressing leakage into non-computational states.
main_result: The proposed Purcell-engineered hybrid coupler significantly reduces leakage probability (down to $1.6	imes10^{-3}$) and improves worst-case gate fidelity ($F_{	ext{min}}=99.62\%$) compared to optimized single-coupler designs.
method: The study employs dressed-eigenstate analysis combined with Lindblad master-equation simulations to model the open quantum system dynamics.
model_or_system: The platform is superconducting qubits (transmons) coupled via a nonlinear transmon coupler, augmented by an engineered subsystem consisting of a Purcell filter and an auxiliary notch resonator. The Hamiltonian describes coherent interactions ($H_{	ext{int}}$), while dissipation is modeled via Lindblad operators.
key_observables: Gate fidelity metrics ($F_{	ext{avg}}, F_{	ext{min}}$) and the leakage probability are the key diagnostics used to quantify gate performance.
important_parameters: The architecture's robustness is tested over a broad range of coherence assumptions and device parameters, with optimized values listed in tables.
main_assumptions: Analysis assumes fixed operating frequencies for qubits and coupler during the gate operation. The notch mode coupling is treated under an approximation hierarchy ($g_{fn} \gg g_{1n}, g_{2n}$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the hybrid coupler, how effective transverse interaction depends on filter frequency, and spectral responses showing engineered dissipation minima near computational transitions.
paper_structure: The paper builds from identifying the leakage problem to proposing the hybrid architecture. It analyzes coherent interactions using dressed-eigenstates, models dissipation engineering via the coupled filter-notch subsystem, and finally validates performance using master equation simulations across varying parameters.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum system dynamics in superconducting circuits by showing how engineered dissipation (the notch/filter) can complement coherent control to achieve higher fidelity gates, which is a key area for AMO physicists studying cavity QED and open systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the Purcell-engineered filter–notch hy- brid coupler. The engineered environment comprises two cou- pled resonant elements: a lossy Purcell-filter resonator F and a weakly dissipative auxiliary notch resonator N. The filter mode couples to the dominant 50 Ωdissipative environment with rate κf, whereas the notch mode couples coherently to the filter through gfn and has only weak intrinsic loss κn. To- gether, the two resonators form a single integrated filter–notch subsystem. Their interference suppresses the environmental response near the computational transitions while retaining a stronger response near selected leakage-related transitions.
